newsitem.title: FRANCE: Britain deserted CJD sufferers - victim's mother.
newsitem.headline: Britain deserted CJD sufferers - victim's mother.

text.p: A mother whose son died of Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease said on Thursday that the British government had deserted CJD victims and their families.
"The relatives feel we've got no one on our side," said Dot Churchill, whose 19-year-old son Stephen died in 1995 from the human equivalent of mad cow disease (BSE).
She said the relatives wanted an independent inquiry into Britain's handling of BSE but British ministers had refused.
The British government had also rejected relatives' request for special nursing facilities for people with CJD, a brain wasting disease thought to result from eating BSE-infected beef.
"(Ministers) think it will just go away," Churchill told Reuters, after putting the relatives' concerns to Euro-MPs and the European Commissioner for health and safety, Padraig Flynn.
The relatives were now considering whether to take legal action against Britain's Ministry of Agriculture, she said.
British epidemiologists said on Wednesday that BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) could kill as many as 80,000 people.
"The government is responsible. They took the risks in the 1980s so they should...pick up the tab," Churchill said.
The families' letters to Britain's political leaders and European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler had received a deeply unsatisfactory response, she continued.
Prime Minister John Major's office had seen no need for special hospital facilities for CJD patients or an inquiry since Britain already had an independent advisory committee on BSE.
"The committee looks ahead at plans and research but it doesn't look back. They obviously don't want to find out what went wrong," Churchill concluded.
Labour Party leader Tony Blair and Farm Commissioner Fischler had not even acknowledged their letters.
Consumer Commissioner Emma Bonino and Flynn had been more supportive, said Churchill, both agreeing the European Union should put a single top official in charge of BSE-CJD.
"At the moment, no one is responsible," she said. "It falls between the three commissioners, Flynn, Bonino and Fischler."

The relatives plan to return to the European Parliament on February 19, when Euro-MPs examine a report from the EU assembly's committee of inquiry on BSE which criticises Britain and the Commission for their handling of the BSE-CJD crisis.
The report was good, Churchill said, but British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg's refusal to testify before the committee of inquiry meant the investigation could not be complete.
On the basis of the report, Euro-MPs may next month recommend legal action against the British government.
